column4: Every creature is under God's grasp at its forelock and the Lord is on a straight path, making the section's unseen holder of the reins almost explicit.
God makes both ships and livestock into conveyances people ride; the mount belongs to a created and divinely fitted order.
On settling upon their backs, riders must remember their Lord's blessing and say that He subjected the mount because they could not master it themselves.
The riding formula ends by naming return to the Lord, giving the section's road and carried rider their final destination.
God says He made livestock for people and they became their owners, directly supplying the ownership side of the section's mount scene.
وَذَلَّلْنَاهَا describes God's subduing livestock so that some become mounts, locating the animal's docility in divine action.
The subdued animals also yield benefits and drink, and the question about gratitude frames that usefulness as a gift.
Livestock carry loads to a land people could reach only with severe personal hardship, so the compliant animal literally makes a hard road passable.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are created for riding, directly naming the animals and purpose developed by the section.
God makes livestock so that people ride some and eat from others, explicitly presenting the ride as His provision.
Livestock meet needs held in people's breasts, and people are carried on them as on ships; the rider's attainment depends on another bearer.
People are carried upon livestock and ships, a concise parallel to the section's human whose passage is made by a bearer.
Sacrificial animals stand, fall onto their جُنُوب, and are described as subjected by God; animal sides and divine submission meet the section's ج ن ب image.
Their flesh does not reach God but human taqwa does, and their subjection calls for magnifying God for guidance, joining the cautious human, subdued animal, and praise.
Abraham asks وَٱجْنُبْنِى وَبَنِىَّ to be kept from idol worship, the exact prayer that the section reads as God leading a mount away from shirk.
God then saves those who practiced taqwa and leaves wrongdoers kneeling in Hell, directly supporting the claim that the cautious do not secure themselves unaided.
Those for whom the best has preceded from God are kept far away from Hell, an especially close nonlexical parallel to being made to pass away from the fire.
Success is defined as being moved away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden, turning rescue into a spatial removal performed upon the person.
God saves those who had taqwa in their place of attainment so that evil does not touch them, naming divine rescue as the outcome of caution.
The people of the Garden rejoice because their Lord وَوَقَاهُمْ from the punishment of Hell, using the protection root with God as protector.
The saved confess that God favored them and وَوَقَانَا from the scorching torment, joining grace, protection, and deliverance from fire.
The blessed are described as having been protected from the punishment of the Blaze, another direct divine enactment of the section's protective stance.
فَوَقَاهُمُ ٱللَّهُ makes God the one who protects the generous and fearful from that Day and meets them with radiance and joy.
The angels ask God to protect believers from evil consequences and declare that whoever He protects that Day has received mercy.
The prayer وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ asks God to do the protecting from fire, matching the section's insistence on protection received rather than self-achieved.
قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا commands active guarding from a fire, the imperative boundary beside 92:17's passive promise of being kept from it.
Whoever has taqwa is promised that God will make his affair ease, directly reuniting the cautious step with divinely supplied yusr.
وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى closely repeats the divine promise to ease a person toward ease, the verbal motion beneath the tractable mount.
God desires yusr for people and does not desire ʿusr, explicitly setting the section's easy and resistant conditions against each other.
God promises to make yusr after ʿusr, presenting hard passage as a condition He can replace with ease.
The assurance that with ʿusr comes yusr states the coexistence that the section distributes between the resistant and compliant journeys.
The repeated assurance fixes yusr beside ʿusr rather than treating difficulty as sovereign over the road.
ثُمَّ ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ says God eases the human being's way, directly combining divine facilitation with a path.
God removes the Prophet's burden, corresponding to the section's concern with what a back can bear without injury.
The removed burden had weighed heavily upon the back, making the non-wounding saddle's secondary sense a concrete human image.
The required cow is لَا ذَلُولٌ, not trained to work the earth or water the field, a Qur'anic boundary case for an animal not broken to human direction.
God makes the earth ذَلُولًا and tells people to walk its slopes, transferring animal tractability to terrain made traversable by Him.
Pilgrims come on foot and on every lean camel through every deep mountain pass, placing the riding animal inside an arduous sacred road.
The poised, swift horses presented to Solomon put both trained stillness and fleet movement into one Qur'anic mount scene.
The panting chargers run at full exertion, a sharp counterpart to the hoof-sore horse that fears placing its foot.
The chargers strike sparks, making hard contact between hoof and ground visible where the section imagines guarded footing on rough earth.
The believers had urged neither horses nor riding camels toward the recovered property; control of the outcome is instead expressly assigned to God.
In danger believers may pray on foot or mounted and must remember God when secure, joining riding, fear, safety, and commanded remembrance.
After settling on the ark, Noah is told to praise God for rescue, a vehicle-mounting formula closely parallel to remembering the Lord upon an animal's back.
Noah says to embark in God's name for the ark's course and anchorage, making the vehicle's movement depend on its Lord.
God carries people by land and sea, while the ship's riders discover in the storm that their smooth passage and rescue are not their own achievement.
The Lord drives ships through the sea so people can seek His bounty, giving divine agency to the motion of the conveyance.
Ship riders call sincerely on God in danger but associate partners after He saves them, reversing the remembrance required upon mounting.
Ships travel through the sea by God's blessing so He may show His signs, explicitly treating conveyance as grace to the patient and grateful.
God can still the wind and leave ships motionless on the sea, exposing the limit of the rider's power over a subjected conveyance.
God subjects ships to run at His command, the maritime form of the animal's bestowed compliance.
A moderate journey would have been followed, but the hard distance deterred the reluctant, turning ease, following, and resistance into a road scene.
The person has not undertaken the steep pass, making moral giving an ascent through resisting terrain rather than an abstract choice.
The question about what the steep pass is holds the road image open for the acts of release and giving that follow.
Skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften to God's remembrance; human yielding is bodily felt and is then named as God's guidance.
Those protected from the stinginess of their own souls succeed, connecting divine و ق ي protection specifically with the giver's opposite, inner avarice.
The command to fear God and spend is followed by the promise that whoever is protected from the soul's stinginess succeeds.
God provides garments that protect from heat and coats that protect in battle, a Qur'anic counterpart to protective equipment that does not wound its bearer.
Moses is warned not to let denial of the Hour turn him aside فَتَرْدَىٰ, so diversion from the directed way ends in the same falling root.
A saved speaker tells his former companion that he nearly أَن تُرْدِينِ, casting the section's fall as ruin toward Hell.
A structure on a collapsing cliff gives way with its builder into Hell, a concrete image of a seemingly usable footing becoming a fatal descent.
The one who associates with God is likened to falling from the sky and being snatched or swept far away, the falling end of refusing Abraham's anti-idolatry route.
The one walking fallen upon his face is set against one walking upright on a straight path, directly testing gait, guidance, and the road's outcome.
Wrongdoers are commanded to be guided to the path of Hell, the terrible reverse of being led alongside and away from the fire.
Disbelievers are driven in companies to Hell, showing an imposed journey whose destination reverses the protective leading in the section.
Those with taqwa are driven in companies to the Garden, a positive procession in which the cautious are conveyed to safety.
Criminals are driven thirsty to Hell, the opposite destination for a group under another's direction.
The command وَٱقْصِدْ فِى مَشْيِكَ calls for a measured gait, a human counterpart to the controlled pace of the section's horse.
The servants of the Merciful walk gently upon the earth, turning faithful yielding into a visible manner of placing one's steps.
Turning one's cheek away and walking exultantly oppose the camel that turns its head toward its rider and the person whose gait is disciplined.
The command فَٱتَّقُوا ٱلنَّارَ tells hearers to guard against the Fire, setting active caution beside the promise that the most cautious will be kept from it.
وَٱتَّقُوا ٱلنَّارَ commands guarding against a prepared fire; 92:17 completes the boundary by assigning actual removal to God.
The wrongdoers have no وَاقٍ against God, defining the limit beyond which no creature can supply its own protective gear or guide.
The condemned person tries to shield the face from terrible punishment, a bodily but futile form of protection opposite divine safe-leading.
Hoarders' foreheads, sides, and backs are branded in Hell; جُنُوبُهُمْ at the fire reverses the image of the cautious being led at the side and away.
Criminals are seized by forelocks and feet, turning the section's guided animal anatomy into coercive capture at judgment.
After denying and turning away, the person goes swaggering to his people, giving rejection the opposite gait from a soft, quickly following mount.
The ban on walking proudly reminds the walker that he cannot split the earth or reach the mountains, checking the illusion that his own stride masters the ground.
The hoarder thinks wealth makes him immortal, matching the false reliance on property immediately before the fall in surah 92.
The hoarder will be cast into the Crusher, turning trust in wealth into an externally imposed plunge.
Livestock offer milk, many benefits, and food before the next ayah names them as carriers, framing transport within a larger embodied blessing.
Livestock are created with warmth, benefits, and food, supplying the creaturely gift within which the riding function appears.
Some livestock are burden-bearers and some close to the ground, a bodily classification that foregrounds animals fitted to human use.
The command to look at how the camel was created invites attention to precisely the creaturely capacities the section draws out.
Solomon's response to the horses binds the mount display to remembrance of his Lord, though the exact force of his statement about love is disputed.
The recalled horses bring legs and necks into view; the precise action is disputed, but these are the same bodily points through which the section depicts pace and response.
The charging animals raise dust, making the ground's response to their fast footfall visible within the continued horse scene.
Those kept far from Hell do not even hear its faintest sound, specifying the completeness of the distance stated in 21:101.
Everyone's coming to Hell is stated as a settled decree; the next ayah's rescue of those with taqwa therefore marks a divinely effected passage through danger.
The faithful pray وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ, another direct request that the Lord supply protection from fire.
Contemplative believers end their prayer with فَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ, assigning the decisive guarding to God.
Servants of the Merciful ask their Lord to turn Hell's punishment away from them, a nonlexical prayer for the same removal.
God protects Pharaoh's believing man from the evils of the plot, showing وَقَى as an enacted rescue rather than merely personal caution.
God turns evil and indecency away from Joseph, a moral counterpart to Abraham asking to be led away from shirk.
Believers are commanded فَٱجْتَنِبُوهُ concerning intoxicants, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows; the same root makes avoidance an enacted separation from idolatrous practice.
Every community receives the call to worship God and اجْتَنِبُوا ٱلطَّاغُوتَ, extending Abraham's requested removal into a universal route away from false worship.
The command فَٱجْتَنِبُوا ٱلرِّجْسَ مِنَ ٱلْأَوْثَانِ uses the root for deliberate distance from idols, the object named in Abraham's prayer.
Those who اجْتَنَبُوا ٱلطَّاغُوتَ from worship and turn to God receive good news, joining avoidance with a changed direction.
For whoever has taqwa, God makes a way out, turning cautious conduct into an exit supplied from beyond the traveler.
Pilgrims are told to take provision, while the best provision is taqwa; caution becomes equipment for an actual journey.
God increases the guided in guidance and gives them their taqwa, supporting the section's sense that even the traveler's caution is bestowed.
The soul is inspired with both its rebellion and its taqwa, treating protective discernment as something given to it.
God does not charge a soul beyond its capacity, a moral analogue to tack that bears without injuring the back.
God has placed no constriction in religion, supporting the section's picture of a divinely fitted rather than needlessly wounding course.
The people of the Garden are introduced with the assurance that no soul is charged beyond its capacity, a boundary on burdens placed upon the traveler.
God makes the earth an expanse for people, preparing the terrain rather than leaving it intrinsically resistant.
The purpose is that people travel broad paths through it, a direct road consequence of the earth's divine preparation.
God makes the earth a resting place and lays paths in it so people may find direction, immediately before the surah's mounting scene.
Freeing a neck is the first meaning assigned to the steep pass, so moral release becomes the act by which difficult terrain is crossed.
Feeding on a day of hunger continues the definition of the steep pass through costly giving.
The orphan of near relation specifies one recipient of the giving that constitutes ascent over the pass.
The destitute person in misery completes the concrete giving by which the steep pass is traversed.
The saved person sees his former companion in the midst of Hell, locating the near-ruin named in the following ayah.
He credits his Lord's favor for not being brought among the condemned, making rescue from the threatened fall a gift.
Those with taqwa are gathered to the Merciful as an honored delegation, forming the safe procession opposite criminals driven to Hell in the next ayah.
Ships plow the sea so people can seek God's bounty and give thanks, another conveyance whose useful motion is assigned to divine provision.
God subjects what is on earth and lets ships run by His command, broadening the subdued-mount claim into a governed world of travel.
God subjects the sea so ships may sail by His command and people may seek His bounty and be grateful.
At sea all invoked powers vanish except God, yet after He brings riders safely to land they turn away, exposing failed remembrance of the carrier's true Lord.
God teaches the making of armor that protects people from violence, a nonlexical parallel to equipment fitted to guard rather than wound.
The person gives only a little and then withholds, a human refusal that contrasts with the fully yielding sense attached to أَعْطَى in the section.
